scenes.narration: Your cat curls up on your lap and starts to purr. It sounds like pure happiness. But scientists say there's a lot more going on.
scenes.visual: A cosy cat on a lap, with a question popping up.

scenes.narration: A purr starts in the voice box. Muscles there twitch open and shut about twenty five times every second, on the breath in and the breath out.
scenes.visual: A throat diagram with vibrating muscles and a big stat.

scenes.narration: Kittens can purr when they're just a few days old, while they're still blind and deaf. It tells their mother, I'm here, and I'm fine.
scenes.visual: A tiny kitten nuzzling its mother.

scenes.narration: Here's the twist. Cats also purr when they're hurt, scared, or even giving birth. So purring isn't only joy. It can be self comfort.
scenes.visual: A worried cat at the vet, still purring.

scenes.narration: Some researchers think it heals, too. Purr frequencies sit between twenty five and one hundred fifty hertz, the same range used to help bones and muscles repair.
scenes.visual: Sound waves washing over a glowing bone.

scenes.narration: And some cats have a trick. They hide a high pitched cry inside the purr, a lot like a baby's. It's hard to ignore, especially at breakfast time.
scenes.visual: A cat staring at an empty food bowl at sunrise.

scenes.narration: So a purr isn't one message. It's a cat's way of saying, I need you, I'm okay, or feed me now.
scenes.visual: The cat back on the lap, ending on the takeaway line.
